idiom_name: hand-written store over Data.define value states with observers (no framework equivalent)
implementation_notes: Ruby's mainstream stack has no consumer for a client-side store: Rails-family applications are server-rendered and stream HTML (Turbo/Hotwire), and objects are mutable by default, so the one-way discipline has no framework support - Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) gives immutable value states and freeze hardens them, but the store, dispatch and subscription plumbing are all hand-written. In-process fan-out is normally expressed as events (dry-events, Wisper, ActiveSupport::Notifications) and per-request state belongs in the controller or session, not in a global store. Where a Flux-style store is genuinely wanted in a Ruby process, the classic structure is justified only as a small explicit class with dispatch and a reducer; the mainstream answer is to keep that layer in the client.
code_sketch:
State = Data.define(:count, :query)            # immutable value state (Ruby 3.2+)
def reduce(state, action)
  case action[:type]
  when :inc    then State.new(count: state.count + 1, query: state.query)
  when :search then State.new(count: state.count, query: action[:query])
  else state
  end
end
# dispatch: state = reduce(state, action); observers.each(&:call)
pitfalls: Rebinding a constant (STORE = reduce(STORE, action)) from a method or a class body warns and can shadow the original; hold the store in one mutable object or a thread-safe container instead of rebinding constants.
Data.define gives value equality but nested collections stay shared; deep-freeze or copy them when snapshots must stay stable.
In a threaded server (Puma, Sidekiq) a global store is shared across requests and threads - per-user state in it leaks between users; keep it per-request or per-session.
Observer callbacks that never unsubscribe become leak and callback-ordering bugs; prefer the framework's event bus (ActiveSupport::Notifications) and unsubscribe explicitly.
alternative: Keep the shared state inside the server-side request cycle: a controller or service object performs the command, updates the model or session and re-renders (Hotwire/Turbo), with an in-process pub/sub bus (dry-events or Wisper) for fan-out. If a client-side store is genuinely required, implement it in the JavaScript layer where a component tree and the Redux tooling exist.
